reason: Nitriding is a well-established thermochemical surface hardening process; this is textbook-level fact in materials science.
Diffusion of nitrogen into the surface layer is the fundamental mechanism of nitriding. Well-established physical fact.
Formation of nitrides (both iron nitrides and alloying element nitrides) is a core part of the nitriding process. Textbook fact.
Standard gas nitriding in ammonia is typically conducted at 500-570°C (some sources say 500-590°C). The range is correct for conventional single-stage nitriding.

Typical holding times for gas nitriding range from 10 to 50+ hours depending on application. The stated range is representative of standard industrial practice, though some processes may go beyond 50 hours.
The depth of the nitrided (diffusion) layer is directly governed by holding time (approximately proportional to √(Dt)). This is a fundamental relationship.
The ε-phase (Fe₂₋₃N) forms at the surface where nitrogen concentration is highest, as predicted by the Fe-N phase diagram. This is well-established in the Lehrer diagram.

Molybdenum nitrides (Mo₂N, MoN) are fine, coherent precipitates that provide significant precipitation (dispersion) hardening during nitriding. Mo is one of the most effective nitriding alloying elements.
Vanadium nitrides (VN) are extremely hard, fine precipitates that provide strong precipitation hardening. VN has very high thermodynamic stability and contributes significantly to hardness.

For standard nitriding regimes (500-570°C, 10-50 h), the diffusion layer depth of 0.3-0.6 mm is typical for many alloy steels. However, exact depth depends strongly on steel composition and specific regime, so this is a reasonable generalization.
XRD is a standard method for phase identification in nitrided layers, and the ε-phase is routinely detected at the surface of gas-nitrided steels. This is a standard analytical result.
The γ'-phase (Fe₄N) is commonly found beneath the ε-phase in the compound layer of gas-nitrided steels and is routinely confirmed by XRD. Standard result.
Vickers microhardness testing with loads of 0.1-0.5 N (HV 0.01 to HV 0.05) is standard practice for measuring hardness profiles in nitrided layers. Typical loads range from 0.05 to 1 N.
Metallographic cross-sections (шлифы) are etched (commonly with nital) to reveal the nitrided layer structure before hardness measurements and microscopy. Standard metallographic practice.
Fick's laws (first and second) are the fundamental equations governing diffusion, including nitrogen diffusion in iron. This is basic solid-state physics.
The temperature dependence of the diffusion coefficient follows the Arrhenius equation D = D₀·exp(-Q/RT). This is a fundamental law of solid-state diffusion.

Literature values for activation energy of nitrogen diffusion in α-iron (BCC) cluster around 76-80 kJ/mol. The value of 77 kJ/mol is consistent with widely cited data (e.g., Fast, Grieve, and others report ~76.1-77.9 kJ/mol). Reasonable and specific.

The pre-exponential factor D₀ for nitrogen in α-iron is reported in literature as approximately 0.003-0.0047 cm²/s (e.g., Fast & Verrijp; Grieve & Jack). The value 0.003 cm²/s is within the accepted range, though some sources give slightly different values. Plausible but source-dependent.

Nitriding does increase wear resistance, and 2-3 times improvement is a commonly cited figure. However, the actual improvement depends heavily on the steel grade, nitriding regime, counter-body material, and wear conditions (abrasive, adhesive, fretting). The claim is directionally correct but oversimplified without specifying test conditions.

Post-oxidation after nitriding (nitrocarburizing + oxidation, e.g., QPQ/Melonite-type processes) does produce a dense oxide film (typically Fe₃O₄ magnetite) that improves corrosion resistance. However, the claim implies oxidation always follows nitriding, which is not universally true — it is a separate, optional process step. The statement lacks context about whether this is a specific process variant being described.
